title: Albert Hofmann makes LSD, 1938 — the molecule left on a shelf for five years
sources: Wikipedia: Albert Hofmann — at Sandoz Laboratories in Basel he studied squill and the fungus ergot; first synthesized LSD on 16 November 1938, aiming for a respiratory and circulatory stimulant; it was set aside for five years until 16 April 1943, when he re-examined it and accidentally discovered its effects; on 19 April 1943 he intentionally took 250 micrograms, which he thought small but was a strong dose; he died aged 102 on 29 April 2008; he said it was misused by the counterculture of the 1960s

Wikipedia: History of LSD — while re-synthesizing it he accidentally absorbed a small amount; 250 micrograms is about 10 times the minimum active amount; he asked his assistant to escort him home and, as was customary in Basel, they went by bicycle — the origin of "Bicycle Day"; Sandoz supplied it to researchers as Delysid from 1947 and halted production in August 1965
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1632 King Gustavus Adolphus is killed at Lützen; 2022 NASA launches Artemis 1
Images: rye ergot (Claviceps purpurea), CC0; the LSD molecule, public domain. No photo of Hofmann or of Sandoz is used
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): a flask, a grain field, a street with bicycles

post.facebook:
On this day in 1938, the Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann first made LSD, at Sandoz Laboratories in Basel.

He was studying ergot, a fungus that grows on rye, and hoped for a medicine to stimulate breathing and circulation. The new compound was set aside. Five years later, on 16 April 1943, he made it again and accidentally absorbed a tiny amount. Three days later he deliberately took a quarter of a milligram — which he thought was small, but was about ten times the amount needed for an effect. He asked his assistant to take him home; as was usual in Basel, they went by bicycle. That ride is now known as "Bicycle Day".

Sandoz supplied the drug to researchers from 1947, but it spread far beyond the lab, and Sandoz stopped making it in 1965. Hofmann lived to 102 and believed his discovery had been misused.

Also on 16 November: King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden was killed at Lützen (1632), and NASA launched Artemis 1 (2022).
